lines.text: Your phone knows where you are, to within a few meters. But it never sends a single signal to space. So how?
About thirty satellites circle twenty thousand kilometers up, each one shouting the same thing: here is where I am, and the exact time I'm saying this.
Your phone only listens. Each signal arrives a fraction of a second late, and that delay is the distance, because radio travels at the speed of light.
Here's the trick, on a flat map. One satellite puts you somewhere on a ring. Two rings cross at two points. A third ring picks the right one. Real GPS does the same, using spheres.
Quick test. Three satellites already pin down your position. So why does your phone listen to four? Backup, accuracy, or the clock? Think!
It's the clock. Radio covers three hundred meters in one microsecond, and your phone's clock is cheap. So the phone treats its clock error as one more unknown. Four unknowns, four satellites.
And here's the wild part. Satellite clocks tick faster than ours, about thirty-eight microseconds a day, thanks to relativity. Uncorrected, GPS would drift about ten kilometers every day.
Two tips. Indoors the signal is weak, so step near a window. And GPS itself uses no data, so download offline maps and navigate anywhere.
Watch again, and count how many satellites it uses.
